title: A purchase split between sister companies
question: Did a department place under-the-limit purchase orders in the same weeks with two or more vendors of one owner-group, adding up to more than the limit?
finding: 5 department-and-vendor pairs show the pattern, 19 times in all: 3 pair(s) tied on record evidence (tiers 1 to 4) and 2 that share only an address. The most frequent: Public Utilities Commsn with Ferguson Enterprises Inc. and Ferguson Waterworks, 5 time(s), 3 of the 16 orders just under the limit. 69,068 delegated purchase orders at or under the limit were tested; in 45 department-and-group combinations two differently named vendors of one group or address pair both received such orders.
how: Purchase orders under the departments’ delegated authority (the file’s "Prop Q" authority), each between $2,500 and the limit in force that year, are grouped by department and owner-group. A cluster is two or more differently named vendors of one group (or one address pair) with orders dated within 14 days of the first, whose amounts add up to more than the limit. The limit is taken from the “split purchases” results: Delegated ("Prop Q") purchasing limit: $10,000 through FY2024, $20,000 from FY2025. "Just under" counts orders in the top tenth below the limit. One row is one department and one set of vendors; the largest single cluster is written out.
limits: The limit is stated in these files per purchase order; whether related vendors must be counted together is not stated and should be checked against the purchasing rules. Two affiliated firms can sell different things, as several of the names suggest, and a department may need both in one fortnight. Several of these rows also show repeated orders to one of the two names alone, which the “split purchases” results already measures. Orders are matched to firms by payee name. The purchase-order extract holds only orders totalling $2,500 to $25,000.
